meta.title: Who really said "You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Augustine: Confessions, Book I, ch. 1. But the Latin has no 'O Lord' in this sentence; the popular English adds it from the opening line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Augustine: Confessions, Book I, ch. 1. But the Latin has no 'O Lord' in this sentence; the popular English adds it from the opening line.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The opening chapter of the Confessions (Book I, ch. 1, written in Latin c. 397–400): “quia fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum donec requiescat in te.” The popular English follows modern renderings such as the one in the Catechism of the Catholic Church. Its “O Lord” comes from the first line of the same paragraph, not from this sentence.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Book I, chapter 1 (I.1.1), the opening paragraph
English text of the Catechism of the Catholic Church, §30 (Libreria Editrice Vaticana)

source.excerpt: You are great, O Lord, and greatly to be praised: great is your power and your wisdom is without measure. … You yourself encourage him to delight in your praise, for you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
trail: The Latin original at The Latin Library ↗, section 1.1.1: “magnus es, domine, et laudabilis valde … quia fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum donec requiescat in te.”

E. B. Pusey’s translation on Project Gutenberg ↗: “Great art Thou, O Lord, and greatly to be praised … for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.” Albert C. Outler’s version at CCEL ↗: “Thou hast made us for thyself and restless is our heart until it comes to rest in thee.”

The Catechism of the Catholic Church, §30 ↗ quotes the passage in the modern wording people now repeat: “for you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you,” and cites Conf. I, I, I.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under the Confessions (I, 1) with its Latin. E. J. Hutchinson’s “Whence St. Augustine’s ‘Restless Heart’?” ↗ found no earlier use of cor inquietum in surviving Latin literature.
source.excerptNote: As quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church, §30, footnote “St. Augustine, Conf. I, I, I.” The Latin reads: “magnus es, domine, et laudabilis valde … tu excitas ut laudare te delectet, quia fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum donec requiescat in te.” “O Lord” (domine) opens the paragraph and does not appear in the famous clause.

source.rightsNote: Augustine’s Latin is centuries old and in the public domain, and so are older English versions such as Pusey’s on Project Gutenberg ↗. The popular modern English, “you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you,” matches modern copyrighted translations such as the Catechism’s English text (© Libreria Editrice Vaticana ↗). So we treat this exact wording as in copyright.

author.name: Augustine of Hippo
author.heading: About Augustine of Hippo
author.metaLine: 354–430 · Bishop of Hippo Regius, Church Father
author.bio: Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was Bishop of Hippo Regius. He is one of the most important Church Fathers of the Latin Church and among the most influential philosophers in Western history. His Confessions, thirteen books written in Latin c. 397–400, is an autobiography framed as a prayer to God, and this line comes from its first paragraph.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The credit to Augustine is correct. What drifts is the English: the version passed around online is spliced together from two parts of his opening paragraph and changes its grammar.

items.who: “… for yourself, O Lord, and our heart …”
items.why: In the Latin ↗ the address domine (“O Lord”) comes in the paragraph’s first words, “magnus es, domine” (“Great art Thou, O Lord” in Pusey ↗). The famous clause itself, “fecisti nos ad te,” contains no “O Lord.”

items.who: “our hearts are restless until they rest in you”
items.why: Augustine wrote cor nostrum, “our heart,” in the singular. Plural renderings are common anyway. Wikipedia ↗ gives “our hearts are restless till they rest in Thee,” and Wikiquote ↗ also lists a plural “O Lord” version.
The “Thou” and “Thee” forms are not errors. They are older translations of the same sentence, such as Pusey’s ↗ (“our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee”).

misattribution.truthLine: Augustine wrote it. In Confessions I.1.1 the line is “quia fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum donec requiescat in te” (Latin text ↗). The most faithful modern English is “you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you,” with no “O Lord.”

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The sentence comes in the first paragraph of the Confessions, before Augustine says anything about his own life. He starts with praise (“Great art Thou, O Lord”) and then gives a reason why a small, mortal creature wants to praise God at all: people were made for God and cannot settle anywhere else. The Catholic Church still uses it this way. The Catechism ↗ quotes it to make the point that God never stops calling people to seek him.

The image seems to be his own. E. J. Hutchinson reports ↗ that he found no instance of cor inquietum, “restless heart,” in surviving Latin literature before Augustine. He concludes that the phrase is probably Augustine’s invention, even if the thought behind it has biblical or philosophical roots.
